newsitem.title: USA: Congress returns from recess to work on budget.
newsitem.headline: Congress returns from recess to work on budget.

text.p: Congress returns from a two-week recess on Monday still seeking a budget agreement with the White House and hoping to step up the pace of a sluggish session.
Majority Republicans who swept into power two years ago are still looking to put their stamp on legislation but are divided over ways to handle key issues of spending and taxes.

Only one bill of any significance has passed since the session began on January 7, an extension of the 10 percent airline ticket tax. Republican-backed constitutional amendments to require a balanced budget and limit congressional terms both failed.

Most major bills are still in committee so there is little for either chamber to do -- a sharp contrast with 1995 when the House voted on 10 major items in the first 100 days of the Congress created by the 1994 election upheaval.

Negotiations between President Bill Clinton and Republican congressional leaders on a package to balance the federal budget by the year 2002 began before the recess, but made little progress. Still, Clinton is talking optimistically.
"I really believe we'll get a bipartisan balanced budget agreement this year. I think it is the right thing to do for the country," Clinton said last week.

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry added: "I think that we always made clear that we want to work real hard to balance the budget, and it would most likely be necessary for the president to talk to the bipartisan leadership at length, if we're going to do so. And he's prepared to do that."
Congress is supposed to pass a measure setting budget resolutions by April 15, but there appears to be little chance that will happen.

One of the key players in the budget talks, House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, spent most of the recess on a trip to China, Hong Kong, Japan and Taiwan. He returns to face growing criticism of his leadership from conservatives who feel he has become too moderate.
They were especially upset when he suggested just before the recess that it might be better to delay a tax cut until a budget agreement is worked out.
Conservatives insist that cuts in personal and capital gains taxes should be part of any budget package.
So intense was the political heat that Gingrich was forced to publicly reaffirm his support for a tax cut.

"You've got to have a tax system that favours economic growth. If you want more jobs and you want more wealth and you want a better future ... there should be no taxes on savings and investments," he said in a speech on Friday.

New York Republican Representative Peter King last week called Gingrich "roadkill on the highway of American politics" in a widely quoted article. Gingrich is also under pressure to pay a $300,000 fine imposed by the House in January for ethics violations and there was speculation he might be forced out.

Besides the budget, other major legislative issues likely to see action soon are a Senate vote on a House-passed bill to ban late-term abortions and a House-Senate effort to reconcile separate measures challenging Clinton's finding that Mexico is a full partner in the war against drugs.
The House wants to revoke his certification while the Senate calls for a six-month review of Mexico's actions.
Clinton is also pressing the Senate to approve a treaty to ban the production, stockpiling and use of chemical weapons by the April 29 ratification deadline.

Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms, a North Carolina Republican, said on Friday he still opposes the pact but is willing to try to resolve his differences with the administration.

The Senate must also confirm the last two of Clinton's second-term nominees, Alexis Herman to be labour secretary and George Tenet to head the Central Intelligence Agency. Tenet replaced Anthony Lake, who withdrew his nomination last month.
